name: Linux Fundamentals
description: Core Linux administration skills covering user management, file permissions, process control, and basic networking diagnostics.

teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
```bash
# Create a new user with home directory
sudo useradd -m -s /bin/bash newuser

# Set the user's password
sudo passwd newuser

# Verify user creation
id newuser
ls -la /home/newuser
```
teachingBlocks.explanation: Linux uses the useradd command to create user accounts. The -m flag creates a home directory, and -s specifies the login shell. User information is stored in /etc/passwd, and password hashes are stored in /etc/shadow. The id command confirms the user exists and shows their UID/GID. Understanding this pattern helps you manage access control across any Linux system.

surfaceVariants.description: Create a system user for running a service (no login shell)
Create user with specific UID for NFS compatibility

hints: Think about what information a user account needs: username, home directory, and shell
The useradd command has flags for each of these - check man useradd
Use -m for home directory and -s for shell specification

commonErrors.description: Used adduser which is a friendlier wrapper but less portable
commonErrors.remediation: While adduser works on Debian-based systems, useradd is the low-level command that works on all Linux distributions
Without -m, the user has no home directory. Many applications expect ~/ to exist.

teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
```bash
# View current permissions
ls -la /path/to/file

# Set permissions using symbolic notation
chmod u+rwx,g+rx,o+r script.sh

# Or using octal notation (equivalent to above)
chmod 754 script.sh

# Change ownership
sudo chown user:group script.sh
```
teachingBlocks.explanation: Linux permissions operate on three levels: user (owner), group, and others. Each level can have read (r=4), write (w=2), and execute (x=1) permissions. The chmod command modifies permissions using either symbolic (u+rwx) or octal (754) notation. Understanding this model is fundamental because it's how Linux controls all file and directory access. Octal notation uses base-8 math: rwx=4+2+1=7.

surfaceVariants.description: Apply permissions recursively to a directory tree

hints: Permissions are shown as 10 characters: type + 3 sets of rwx
r=4, w=2, x=1 - add them up for each position

commonErrors.remediation: 777 is almost never appropriate - it allows anyone to modify the file. Use 755 for executables and 644 for regular files.
Remember: first digit is owner (u), second is group (g), third is others (o)

teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
```bash
# View running processes
ps aux | head -20

# Real-time process monitoring
top -bn1 | head -20

# Find specific process
pgrep -a nginx

# Send signal to process
kill -SIGTERM $(pgrep nginx)

# Force kill if needed
kill -9 <pid>
```
teachingBlocks.explanation: Every running program in Linux is a process with a unique PID. ps shows process snapshots, top provides real-time monitoring, and kill sends signals to processes. SIGTERM (15) asks a process to terminate gracefully, while SIGKILL (9) forces immediate termination. Understanding process management helps you diagnose performance issues and manage system resources.

data.command: systemctl status nginx && systemctl restart nginx

hints: ps aux shows all processes with detailed info
Use pgrep to find process IDs by name

commonErrors.description: Immediately used SIGKILL without trying SIGTERM
commonErrors.remediation: SIGKILL doesn't allow cleanup. Always try SIGTERM first and wait before using -9
Always verify the PID with ps or pgrep before sending kill signals

teachingBlocks.canonicalSolution:
```bash
# Check network interfaces
ip addr show

# Test connectivity
ping -c 3 google.com

# Check DNS resolution
host google.com

# View routing table
ip route show

# Check listening ports
ss -tulnp
```
teachingBlocks.explanation: Network diagnostics start with checking your interfaces (ip addr), testing connectivity (ping), verifying DNS (host), and examining routes. The ss command replaces netstat for viewing socket statistics. Understanding this diagnostic flow helps you systematically troubleshoot connectivity issues from layer 1 (physical) through layer 7 (application).
hints: Start with ip addr to see if interfaces are up
ping tests basic connectivity; if it fails, check routing
ss -tulnp shows what's listening and which process owns each port

commonErrors.remediation: ifconfig is deprecated. Use ip addr, ip route, ip link for modern Linux networking
ss is faster and more feature-rich than netstat. Learn ss -tulnp
